source_text: Non dubito eiusmodi opinionem hactenus super nostro fuisse certamine, ut ad quaestionem involutam magis, quam ad summam spectare fidei crederetur. Procul quippe ab studiis spiritalibus agitantes, solis famae aurulis commoventur; temporumque formidantes invidiam, nec compertae veritatis praesidium tenentes (ut fere in rebus trepidis, nulli minus quam sibi creditur), tutius iter, quod frequentius, arbitrantur.
pass_a_gloss: I do not doubt that an opinion of this kind has thus far been upon our contest, that it was believed to look more to an involved question than to the sum of faith. For those agitating far from spiritual studies are moved by the little breezes of fame alone; and fearing the spite of the times, not holding the protection of a found truth (as generally in fearful matters, it is trusted to none less than to oneself), they judge the safer road that which is more frequent.
pass_b_english: I do not doubt that until now our dispute has been regarded as concerning an obscure question rather than the heart of the faith. People living far from spiritual pursuits are moved only by passing breezes of rumor. Fearing the hostility of the times and lacking the protection of verified truth—as commonly happens amid alarm, when people trust no one less than themselves—they think the more crowded road the safer one.

choices.why: Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
